Selling vol has two awesome features:
1. You start from a well-defined edge
2. You don't have to be smart to do it

Being smart is actually counter-productive.

The more intelligent you are, the more you can fool yourself. You might think that your discretion adds value. That you can manage complexity. That you can cleverly avoid drawdowns.

Start from the assumption that you don't know anything, except:
1. The variance risk premium exists
2. The only way to harvest it, is systematically

So you need consistency, simplicity, and risk tolerance.

Consistency because volatility trades are individually volatile. You need a large enough sample to beat randomness.

Simplicity because your system needs to be measurable. For every decision rule, think about whether it complicates the feedback loop.

Risk tolerance because you need to handle drawdowns. They're inevitable. Position size accordingly. Don't overwrite the rules to try to prevent a drawdown. Don't rewrite the rules every time a drawdown happens.

If you start treat volatility selling with humility and discipline, you will inevitably make money.

@BitlightLabs has released the latest update on staying in sync with Lightning development progress, while also introducing several new features planned for future support.

@rgbstashlabs provides an in-depth explanation of two key features from this roadmap, along with further context on their significance for Stash Labs products such as https://t.co/wbBpe7HUch, RLSP, and Flash Dex.

🔥 Two Core Capabilities Explained:

• JIT liquidity for RGB: just-in-time RGB asset channel opening
• Splice for RGB: dynamic capacity adjustment of RGB asset channels

Building on our RLSP + Atomic Swap capabilities, https://t.co/wbBpe7HUch is about to launch native asset swap trading. However, the current RGB Lightning Network pipeline has key pain points:

When a user completes a $RGB buy order via RLN and RLSP, two channels must be opened sequentially:

✅ User opens a BTC channel to pay BTC to the RLSP
✅ RLSP opens a BTC/RGB composite channel to deliver $RGB to the user

Three Major Drawbacks of the Current Model:

1⃣ Dual channel opening requires waiting for Bitcoin mainnet block confirmations — typically 6 confirmations — resulting in extremely high transaction latency.
2⃣ Channel capacity is fixed. Once the balance is insufficient for the next transaction, the old channel must be closed and a new one rebuilt — a costly process with high fees and a fragmented user experience.
3⃣ The current model is completely unable to support high-frequency continuous trading scenarios like FlashDex perpetual contracts, severely limiting the RGB ecosystem's trading experience.

🚀 JIT Liquidity | On-Demand RGB Channel Opening
JIT (Just-In-Time) liquidity — the core principle is to create on demand, with no pre-lockup required:
▸ Users don't need to pre-fund or manually create RGB asset channels;

▸ When initiating a $RGB receive/swap request, the RLSP instantly generates a virtual off-chain channel — no immediate on-chain settlement needed;
▸ After the first transaction is completed, it is automatically anchored on-chain and converted into an official RGB Lightning channel.

💡 Core Value:

• Zero-barrier entry to RGB asset swaps — no idle capital lockup.
• Dramatically reduced transaction wait times, eliminating mainnet block confirmation delays.
• Enables users to complete $RGB transactions as seamlessly as Lightning BTC, while maximizing RLSP capital efficiency.
🛠 Splice for RGB | Dynamic Capacity Adjustment for RGB Asset Channels

Built on the Lightning Network's native Channel Splicing technology, allowing RGB asset channels to be resized without closing or rebuilding:
▸ Splice-in (expand): Add BTC/RGB assets directly to an existing channel;

▸ Splice-out (shrink): Withdraw idle funds from the channel as needed;
▸ The channel remains uninterrupted throughout — no trading pauses required. Only the funding transaction is updated via signatures, requiring a single on-chain confirmation.

💡 Core Value:

• Permanently eliminates the old pattern of "close and reopen a channel when the balance runs out".

• Seamlessly supports high-frequency continuous trading, enabling FlashDex perpetual contract scenarios.
• Significantly reduces on-chain fees from repeatedly opening/closing channels, improving capital turnover and utilization.
🔗 Synergy of Three — Redefining the https://t.co/wbBpe7HUch Atomic Swap Experience
• RLSP + Atomic Swap: Powers the underlying asset swap logic.

• JIT: Solves the "0 to 1" problem — no pre-built channels, instant trade initiation.

• Splice: Solves the "1 to N" problem — dynamic channel scaling to support high-frequency continuous trading.

With JIT + Splice landing together, the current pain points of RGB channels — high latency, cumbersome workflows, and the inability to support high-frequency trading — will be fully resolved. This lays a solid infrastructure foundation — high performance, low barriers, and high liquidity — for https://t.co/wbBpe7HUch's upcoming Atomic Swap and ecosystem derivatives trading. 🚀

It is worth noting that these two features will not affect the https://t.co/wbBpe7HUch launch timeline — they serve purely as a leap forward in user experience.

– Place orders at existing price levels. If I see someone opened an order at $0.35 for $50, I'll place my order at that same price. I do this so if someone wants to sell at $0.35, their order fills faster and with higher probability than mine.

– Open orders on 20-30 markets simultaneously to earn rewards from everywhere.

– Check each order frequently to make sure it's not approaching the mid price and getting filled unexpectedly.

– Always use only half my balance for orders. This ensures that if one order fills, the other orders don't get canceled and continue farming.

– Check notifications constantly to see if any of my orders filled unexpectedly.

– Always check market end dates. If a market ends in less than 24 hours, be careful—you could lose money.

– Avoid highly volatile markets. You can also lose money on those.

These are my core principles that I use. Hope this was helpful!

Food for thought: A $10M call buy can be a bearish stock-replacement trade

Worth thinking about what I state above before you "follow the whale."

If a big call purchase is a stock replacement trade, is it bullish or is it bearish? 

It's actually bearish, right? Because the guy's reducing his delta. The motivation for an insto to buy a big call option, which to you looks like "oh my God, someone just spent $10 million of premium," might be because he just sold $200 million of stock and now he's replacing it with calls.
 
Let's say I'm an institution. I've got $200 million of stock, I've run it up, I've made money. Let's say I bought it at the lows at $150, and now I'm looking at this resistance at $210 going, we might just reject it again. I don't want to give all my money back.
 
So I bank the $200 million of stock. And I spend some of the money I made, maybe $10 million on some calls in case the thing wants to fly. That gets me back into my position. 

To you, you're going to see that as a bullish insto flow, but it's not at all a bullish insto flow. It's quite a bearish one. Because the guy is banking stock he's owned since 40% ago and going from 100% delta long to maybe only 30%.

That's the problem with reading flow off the tape. You're not going to see the stock sale. You're just going to see the call buys...

Here is a tactic from the banking desk that travels to retail, but the tools change.

When I'd see a client I was providing liquidity to and I knew I was going to lose money on the trade, I'd just cut the trade quickly, take the loss, and then follow the guy and go the same way. Because 9 times out of 10 he would be right due to some superior information.

What I wanted from my salespeople, and they were terrible at giving it to me, was add some value and track how good my clients' hit rates were. Show me which ones are good at calling the market, which ones are terrible. Then I can use that to position my own book.

Now in retail, it's even harder. We don't know who the clients are, we don't know why they're doing the trade, we don't know anything if we're honest with ourselves.

Which means the only signal you've got is what the print does to the surface. That's the retail tool for the same habit.

I see it thru fixed-strike vol on the screen via Vol bid, skew shifts, surfaces moving. That tells me if dealers are scrambling. And if they are scrambling, it means they don't want to take the other side of that flow.

Question I get a lot: which VIX product should I use?

For me there's only two things you can actually trade.

You trade the monthly VIX option, which settles into the cash level of that VIX future expiring on the same day. So there's no mismatch between the option expiry and what it settles into. It's cash settled, it's priced off that maturity VIX future, and it's very liquid because you can trade gazillions of it.

Or you trade VXX weeklies, which are physical delivery into the VXX ETF. You never let them run till expiry. You always roll them or exit them before the actual expiry day. Liquidity is relatively decent enough.

Anything else on VIX is a waste of time, in my opinion. Too wide, too opaque. No idea what's going on in those screens.

That's it.

You might be good at calling direction in a name. Or you might not.

You'll find out by looking back at your trades. That's the only way to actually know whether your edge is real or imaginary. We have a habit of kidding ourselves.

Conviction in the moment doesn't tell you. The receipts do.

Fixed-strike vol shows the footprint of flow, not just the flow

The reason I've created all my under-the-hood metrics is because I want to see the market impact of the flow. 

Seeing the flow is one thing, but if it didn't move the option surface and got absorbed easily then did it really matter? 

If it actually made a proper footprint on the market, meaning liquidity providers got taken the other side even though they might not naturally want to be. That's what I care about more.
 
If that big print was actually a smart-money person who knew something, the dealers are going to be scrambling on the other side of it. 

And the only way you see that is by tracking, has the skew shifted a lot after this flow? Has the fixed-strike vol gone up or down after this flow?
 
We saw it in all these breakout stocks. $INTC was rallying, skew was going ballistic for calls, vol was going bid. $AMD same. $QCOM same.

Layering delta, theta, vega: the orthogonal alpha stack in options

How I think about putting a book together. Not one trade. Layers.

The idea is you've got directional alpha. You might be good at calling direction in a name, right? You'll find out by looking back at your trades. But if you then layer on theta as another alpha, where there's evidence of the street being long gamma, there are smart ways to earn theta safely. Calendars, diagonals, whatever. That's something that actually funds the things that aren't going so well.
 
When the delta picks aren't working because the market's maybe not moving enough, it's probably because markets are quite range-bound, and you're nicking a bit of theta out of your theta trades.
 
And similarly on the vega side, when you start doing more vega trades, those become orthogonal to the directional trades and the theta trades because they're all about implied vol. They're quite theta-neutral. They don't really care that much about spot direction, they're using the mean-reversion properties of vol.
 
Once you've got all those layers operating together, chances are over time you're going to do quite well. That's the idea.

The longer you stay in low vol, the harder it is to break out of low vol.

Open interest is just a number. What matters is who owns it.
 
10,000 contracts owned by one institution that always rolls is a pin you can lean on. They behave predictably, the strike behaves predictably, the vol surface around it tells you when they're about to move. There is a footprint on the surface consistent with the trade and the positioning of dealers the other side.

The JPMorgan put spread collar that rolls every quarter? Whole street knows the timing. Vol front-runs it. That's a tradeable pattern.
 
However, same 10,000 contracts scattered across 200 retail accounts, that's noise. 

Some exercise late, some don't exercise at all, some get assigned by accident. The strike behaves randomly.
 
This is why dividend trades, expiry pins, and strike-magnet patterns work better in stocks with concentrated institutional flow than in retail favourites.

What we can do, is show the chart, and tell you what happened before.

Grid bots are a valuable liquidity service to the market.

You should expect to get paid for it.

But you're taking the risk of short trend, short vol. Similar to a short straddle. You need prices that mean-revert in a range.

That's statistically more likely on weekends. Saturdays especially. Vol usually picks up by the time Asia re-opens. So a sensible idea would be to deploy the bot from Friday 17h to Sunday 17h (UTC).

How do we set the grid range?

Pure laziness. The options market needs to come up with vol estimates, so we'll just copy their homework. Take implied volatility on friday, scale it by √(2/365), and add a multiplier to taste. Apply this to either side of the weekend open price and you have your grid range. We used a multiplier of one, which means setting the range equal to one standard deviation.

What about the end of the weekend?

For the chart below, we close whatever position we built up. Nothing prevents you however from using the grid around a long spot position, to create a DCA enhancement.

How did grid-as-a-service perform on the weekend shift?

In the last 11 weekends, it made money in 9 of them, and returned ~30% on margin. Small sample, presumably not reflecting true risk, but suggestive of potential nonetheless.

The two losing weekends happened on the uptrend from 70-80k. That's to be expected. We're short drift. A trend filter or skew adjustment to the grid would be logical areas to look for improvement.

BTC price with 14-day implied vol:
• Jul'25 is the bull case
• Jan'26 is the bear case

P.S. interesting contrast:
• Jan'25 high printed on a vol expansion (66% IV)
• Oct'25 high ended on low percentile vol (36% IV) https://t.co/ICCV6KRG56

A volatility cone shows where current implied and realized vols sit relative to the historic distribution of realized.

This cone uses two years of BTC close-to-close (8am utc) with realized-vol windows aligned to the time-to-maturity of different option expiries.

What do we see?

IVs sit well below the 2Y-median, with front IVs bordering on the 25th percentile. So they're historically cheap but nothing extreme.

There is an RV vs IV crossover. At the front, 7-day IV (34%) is still a chunky premium over 7-day realized (~30%). At the back, 224-day IV at 45% is slightly below realized, which still reflects shocks from earlier this year.

So implieds have simply smoothed out the RV trend, and are pricing in that short-term vol compression will normalize.

The idea of buying short-dated expiries is not necessarily attractive. For instance, the 29-May straddle with 13 days to go, still quotes you a break-even move of 76-85k. You need a range break for it to make money.

The more attractive part of the curve is arguably the longer-dated side where you can lock in sub-40 IV entries with less theta, and more vega.

Blue is the colour of BTC 14-day realized vol being ≤ 30%. It's 28% right now. That's a 6% rank over the last two years.

Historically, this level of vol compression announced major resistance. The pattern was that there'd be one last squeeze, then death.

The window used to measure volatility matters of course. We didn't do anything scientific here. Picked 14 days because it's a nice balance of leading but not being too early.

What does it all mean?

Not much in isolation. It's a one-dimensional metric overlaid on a price chart. Anecdotal at best. It does raise an interesting question: should you "mechanically" buy puts when vol gets low enough?

They don't feel attractive to buy, do they?

Maybe that's precisely the point. People tend to buy puts when they get scared. They like to react to something, which can be a good trade, but you will inevitably buy vol at higher levels than right now... when nothing is happening.

Hence, you could approach buying vol as a "why not" more than a "why" question. Maybe it's as simple as buying a little when implied ranks cheap and realized gets very compressed.

This chart shows 7-day BTC ATM IV plotted against 7-day look-ahead RV, sampled daily at 8:00 utc, with data going back to Oct'24.

What do we see?

Usually, IV > RV.
The dotted line separates positive from negative volatility risk premium (VRP). 66% of observations fall below the line. This is the basic short-vol edge: most of the time, implied volatility overstates future realized.

But IV - RV is left-skewed.
While positive VRP observations are more frequent, negative VRP observations have larger outliers. That is the long-gamma payoff profile: lose small repeatedly, then get paid when realized volatility jumps.

IV forecasts RV, but low IV is not the same as cheap vol.
Higher IV generally lines up with higher forward RV, so IV contains information about future RV. That doesn't mean that low IV is good value. There are plenty of positive VRP observations while IV ranks low.

Low IV does not mean RV is likely to outperform.
In this sample, IV readings below 35% did not coincide with a higher likelihood of RV outperformance. If anything, the opposite. This doesn't mean selling low IV is a good idea either. We cannot observe what didn't happen. Logically, low IV means taking relatively more gamma risk so even if this paid off in-sample, it might not have been enough for the potential risk.

Final note:

This chart compares volatilities, but variance is more relevant.
Vol was a bit easier on the eyes. However, the P&L of a (delta-hedged) straddle actually scales with the variance risk premium: IV^2 - RV^2. On that basis, the same volatility difference can have a different impact. A 30 IV versus 50 RV miss is `900 vs 2,500`, a variance gap of `1,600`; a 60 IV versus 80 RV miss is `3,600 vs 6,400`, a variance gap of `2,800`. Both are 20-vol misses, but the second is larger in variance terms.

The sweet spot is an efficient inefficient exchange.

For execution, you want efficient: low fees, low latency, reliable APIs.

For flows, you want inefficient: the taker flow needs to be soft (e.g. retail yoloing options with funded accounts) while being small enough to stay below the radar of the largest MMs.

Black & Scholes gives risk-neutral option prices.

The expected return of the underlying is irrelevant as it's hedged away to create an arbitrage-free price.

However, if you trade an option without hedging, then the expected return certainly does matter. How can you reconcile this with the option prices you're quoted?

You can modify Black & Scholes to accept a drift parameter. Sinclair explains this in Positional Option Trading. This adjusted formula lets you translate a directional view into a subjective option price.

Here's a tool that implements it:
https://t.co/xaHG8kpix5

You can input an estimated forward price for a given expiration. Drift gets inferred from that.

You can also input a variance risk premium to account for the drag of IV potentially being overstated.

You'll find that, in absolute terms, ITM/ATM strikes get more lift from a higher forward whereas OTM strikes tend to get a larger relative multiplier.

the half life of LP equity in a trending regime is short, and it gets shorter as size scales because the OI cap trails realised OI rather than leading it.

then the debt queue activates. 

martingaler issues claims paid by the next loser. once the queue is observable, the EV of opening a new position is negative twice: once because winners get haircut, once because withdrawals sit behind every prior bust. rational flow stops. Queue does not clear.

The mental models are similar.

If you sell an option and hedge, you're creating a bet on the difference between implied and realized volatility. This is delta-neutral in first order, but it tends to have directional exposure due to spot-vol correlation.

If you sell a future and hedge with a perp, you're creating a bet on the difference between implied and realized funding. This is delta-neutral in first order, but it tends to have directional exposure due to spot-basis correlation.

This may sound counterintuitive, but when implied vol is high, it's often not attractive to sell. The variance risk premium often compresses or even turns negative.

Think about it in simple terms. For IV to be pushed above average, something must be happening. Either RV spiked, as in early February, or the market is reacting to news events, as in early March. In both cases, the odds of higher RV increase going forward: volatility has short-term momentum, while uncertainty can force changes in positioning.

There is also a technical reason. IV reflects volatility priced across a distribution of possible outcomes. By contrast, RV is measured along a single path. It's a draw from the distribution, which can get more extreme.

Selling vol is hard to time and success will vary on a trade-by-trade basis. If IV looks rich, RV can easily overshoot. If IV > RV, you can still lose because hedging is path-dependent. The edge in vol selling is therefore something you need to realize systematically across many trades.

If we do try to delineate regimes, then arguably moderate IV, especially when vol starts to trend down, is a better setup than fading IV just because it's ranking above its long-term average.

If you sell a future against a perp, you have a delta-neutral trade that depends heavily on the index price.

Contradiction?

Let's take an extreme example. You sold futures at 120k spot, 8% annual basis, and entered a long perp to hedge.

When you sold that future, you locked in basis as an absolute dollar-amount of ~$4k using a March future.

Then the index price went down. 

The perp leg got charged funding rate * index progressively. Even if the funding rate were constant at 8% annual as well, the index price on which it applies averaged down, so you still get + carry.

Then there is correlation between price and carry. As price goes down, rates compress.

Basis went from 8% to 0% and funding rates went down as well. That's an additional directional lever. Basis gets marked lower (+ pnl) and funding cost decreases (also + pnl).

So futures spreads are quite directionally levered through (1) debasement and (2) re-rating.

Delta-neutral delta.

That's what makes these interesting to trade in my opinion.

Option implied probabilities are kind of ‘dumb’.

Or better said, intelligent in a narrow sense.

Market makers fit option prices to a volatility surface. Their main goal is internal consistency: prices across strikes and expiries must be coherent so they cannot be mechanically arbitraged.

Those prices imply a risk-neutral distribution whose mean is the forward price. Under no-arbitrage pricing that forward reflects carry, not expected returns. Market makers delta hedge, they don’t need to forecast spot to price options.

So the distribution implied by options is not meant to predict the possible paths of spot. It is not a “real-world” distribution but a pricing device that keeps quotes arbitrage-free.

That is why it can miss context a discretionary trader sees: a level of support that is held, momentum building, which range high is likely to be retested. Options prices only adapt to these dynamics when positional traders lift orders.

Hence, you should feel free to disagree with implied probabilities.

For example, the BTC 27-Mar 80k call has a 9 % risk-neutral probability of expiring in the money. Say you assign a 60 % chance of moving up, and conditional on moving up you give a ⅓ chance of finishing above 80k. Your subjective probability is 20 %, and you see value in buying the call.

They sound like a good idea when volatility term structure gets inverted: "Sell expensive IV in the front, buy cheap IV in the back."

But that's not the exposure you get with a calendar.

Let's look at an example from the fast market on Feb 5th. Say that, with btc at 60k, you sold the 20-Feb 60k call and bought the 27-Mar 60k call.

You sold a call for ~90% IV and bought a call for ~70% IV.

Why is this a losing trade?

Delta
The Feb call is relatively more sensitive to a change in underlying price. The calendar was initially ± Δ-neutral, but as the market recovered, the Δ of the call in Feb went up more than the call in Mar, so you picked up a short delta position.

Vega
Options with longer maturities have more vega. This makes the calendar net long vega. In essence, you're long forward vol between Feb and Mar. How could you expect to make money on that if you locked in Mar vol at 70?

As IV shifted down in parallel across the term structure, the vega P&L started bleeding.

When you delta-hedge, your two basic approaches are:
1. Hedging at a regular time interval
2. Hedging based on a delta tolerance

Delta tolerance seems logical, but it has problems. You risk over-trading during volatility spikes because vanna amplifies delta swings on jumps in implied vol. You might force yourself to trade exactly when books widen.

Time-based hedging is simple but also arbitrary. It works reasonably well if you have a diverse book of options where delta changes get smoothed, but you should refine it if you look at hedging/replicating single positions.

My preference is threshold-based hedging. You'll hedge only if a threshold change in delta persists for a minimum period of time. Think of it as a debounce filter based on both time and delta. 

This stops you from over-hedging choppy mean reversion. It does introduce the risk of reacting too slowly to genuine breakouts, but this can be managed by keeping a (wider) delta tolerance as a backstop.

- this rule doesnt cause casino to go bankrupt

昨晚美股 COIN 和 HOOD 逆市拉升，核心驱动力就是这份在参议院银行委员会“强行闯关”的《CLARITY法案》（加密货币市场结构法案）。

简洁拆解一下，这份法案本质上是给币圈发了一张“免死金牌”：

1. 核心逻辑：明确“裁判是谁”
长期以来，美国加密行业处于 SEC（证监会）和 CFTC（商品期货委员会）的“双重毒打”之下。

法案目的： 划清界限。明确哪些币属于“数字商品”（归 CFTC 管），哪些属于“证券”（归 SEC 管）。

利好点： 绝大多数去中心化代币将被定性为商品。这意味着 SEC 那个以加里·根斯勒为首、处处刁难行业的“监管大棒”被强行没收了。

2. 政治风向：两党共识的初步达成
图里有个细节：13名共和党全赞成，甚至有2名民主党议员“反水”倒戈支持。

这标志着加密监管不再是单纯的党派斗争，而是逐渐转向“合规竞争”。

即便反加密急先锋 Elizabeth Warren 坚决反对，也挡不住大势。法案进入参议院全体表决，是行业合法化的重大利好。

3. 市场影响：从“草台班子”到“正规军”
对 Coinbase/Robinhood： 逻辑非常简单。以前是“违法经营”的风险溢价，现在是“持牌收税”的确定性估值。一旦法律边界清晰，机构资金进场就再无合规障碍。

对行业： 以前是靠“信仰”和“情绪”炒币，以后要看“合规”和“法务”。

知乎式总结：
《CLARITY法案》的进展，意味着加密货币正在从华尔街的“法外之地”变成“合法狩猎场”。

如果你持有 COIN 或相关标的，这波涨幅本质上是在给“确定性”定价。 监管虽然收紧了，但“有法可依”远比“无法无天”对大资金更有吸引力。

3 Trading Paradigms That Have Exceptional Merit

While I don't claim to have it all figured out, I have traded a lot over the years and I have identified 3 trading paradigms that I think have exceptional merit.

Campaign and Position Trading
My biggest wins have came position trading. The problem with position trading is that it is capital intensive and has a high risk of drawdown. 

The fix is to turn position trading thesis into "campaigns". The fundamental difference is campaigns focus on active management of a long term position. The management can come in different flavors but typically involve trading around the core position (averaging in and out) and utilizing options.

The stress of this kind of methodology is that it is ongoing.  This form of trading can offer the highest absolute return on capital. The catch is that very large drawdowns are still a real possibility: to make it robust requires portfolio level risk management with particular attention to the products traded.

Organic / Discretionary / Process-Driven High Volume Trading

This is the least well-defined bucket on my list. But, I think there is value in placing lots of trades that cannot be learned by other methods because trading the immediate market is the truest form of expression. In my mind, the volume is what is most important which is contrary to what most retail traders learn.

Why? Yes placing more trades allows for more "reps" and faster learning. But, there's something deeper which is how markets function.

The tricky part is how do you capture that value without losing too much.  The most conservative way is to trade on the simulator and only trade ideas that are verified with real money. 

The other path is organic scaling and process development: the most important risk management is to only scale with your closed profits.  With any discretionary trading, it is typical that most accounts are blown over a few losing days therefore risk management is critical.

Systematic Trading
Now everyone knows about systematic trading. And, I used to think it gave the highest probability of marginal success but the lowest probability of exceptional translation.  But, that was probably untrue then and is even more untrue now with the capabilities available. Exceptional translation is up to the trader.

There you have it: 3 trading methodologies that have exceptional merit. Let me know your thoughts!

Concentration Risk: This Is Not a Broad Market Rally.

That is why I think some caution is warranted here. Under the surface, this has not been a clean, evenly distributed bull market. Technology stocks alone accounted for roughly 85 percent of the S&P 500’s return, while the S&P 500 excluding technology rose just 3 percent. That is not broad participation. That is a handful of giants dragging the index higher by the collar.

The biggest example is NVIDIA (NVDA). NVDA now represents roughly 9 percent of the S&P 500 by market value and has contributed about 20 percent of the index’s total return this year. That is incredible leadership, but it is also concentration risk. If NVDA catches a cold, a lot of the index weight catches a cold with it.

This does not mean the rally has to fail. It means the market is leaning very hard on one theme, one sector, and now one stock at the center of the AI complex. That works beautifully until it stops working beautifully.

Hans’s Take

The market is not broken. But it is stretched. But it isn't what I'd call 'broadly healthy'. And when the rubber band stretches this far, it can snap back with a bang, not a whimper.

Sure, earnings are terrific, but a lot of that traces back to AI.

There is still strong momentum in AI and semiconductors, and momentum can carry much farther than reasonable people expect. But when rates rise, oil rises, and inflation data gets hotter, the margin for error shrinks.

This is exactly the kind of environment where options discipline matters. Don’t confuse a strong trend with a risk-free trend. That is how people become the Thanksgiving turkey — great track record, right up until the wrong Thursday.

You may think that based on all the Teslas out there that oil ain't so important anymore, but it is the hidden building block for over 6,000 everyday products. Everything from your morning medicine to the food you eat and the clothes you wear relies heavily on petrochemical derivatives. 

💊 Medicine & Health

Modern healthcare relies on petroleum byproducts to keep both life-saving and routine medical supplies accessible.

Pain Relievers & Drugs: Common medications like Aspirin utilize benzene, a hydrocarbon derived from petroleum.

Medical Equipment: Vital items like IV bags, syringes, artificial limbs, hearing aids, and heart valves are made from oil-based polymers.

Hygiene Products: Contact lenses, dentures, and the active ingredients in your hand lotion and toothpaste (like polyethylene glycol) all start with oil.

🍔 Food & Agriculture

It might be hard to stomach, but fossil fuel derivatives are everywhere in your kitchen.

Artificial Flavors: Many synthetic flavorings, particularly vanillin (vanilla) and benzaldehyde (almond flavor), are engineered from petroleum.

Food Preservatives: Preservatives like TBHQ (tertiary butylhydroquinone) keep packaged potato chips and crackers from spoiling, and they are sourced from petroleum.

Fertilizers: Ammonia, an essential ingredient in nitrogen-based fertilizers used for global food production, is produced using natural gas and petroleum feedstocks.

👗 Fashion & Textiles

Most synthetic fabrics that dominate our closets are spun from oil.

Synthetic Fibers: Polyester, nylon, spandex, and acrylic are all petroleum-based materials. These oil byproducts give your sportswear and everyday clothing lightweight, water-resistant, and wrinkle-free properties.

Oil is the foundation for countless household goods and grooming products.

Interesting that not a single person on this thread understands why this is a horrible idea.

The original rationale for private investments was that they had an illiquidity premium. That is, they offered a higher return in exchange for giving up liquidity.

You can make the argument that as they become more liquid and more popular, the asset class gets bid up and the risk premium for being illiquid goes away.

That is, the expected return and degree of liquidity converge with public markets over time.

And then privates are not necessarily a "great place to be" any more as you can just sit in publics and get the same deal.

Every agentic platform fits the backtest in-sample and ships the screenshot. 

the strategy dies in production for the same 4 reasons every time:

1. No walk-forward - fit and ship on the same candles

2. Survivorship bias - tested on the assets that survived

3. zero fees, zero slippage - the edge eats itself in live

4. 1 regime - built in a bull tape, run in a chop

HyperSignals V2 enforces walk-forward by default. 

Out-of-sample windows across 3 market regimes.

Crypto Market Making & The Cold Start Problem with John Gu (Caladan)

My guest today is John Gu, founder and CEO of Caladan, one of the most active market makers in crypto and a firm that has provided liquidity to more than 200 token launches. John's path runs through MIT, AlphaSimplex, Citadel's principal strategies group, and Tower Research before landing in Singapore at the dawn of the ICO era — where what started as a trade on the kimchi premium became the foundation for one of the most active liquidity providers in digital assets.

The thesis of our conversation is what I'll call the cold start problem. In traditional markets, every newly listed stock arrives with scaffolding already in place — a designated market maker, a reference price, a universe of comparables, and decades of regulatory infrastructure. Crypto inverts that. A new token can launch with no orderbook, no comparables, and no clear demand curve. Someone has to quote a two-sided market into that void, and how they do it shapes whether the asset becomes a real, tradable thing — or a graveyard of wide spreads and stranded liquidity.

John and I dig into how you bootstrap liquidity from zero, how the quoting playbook evolves as a market matures, the economics of token market making contracts, and how that same infrastructure now bridges into structured products and treasury solutions for token foundations.

Please enjoy my conversation with John Gu.

We are issuing an important correction to our previous announcement regarding the Ribbon DOVs exploit. Our initial analysis was fundamentally flawed, and we owe our community both an apology and an explanation.

In our urgency to respond to the exploit, we failed to properly understand the funds allocation before communicating. This led us to publish a resolution framework that, as it turns out, does not reflect reality. This was a mistake on our part: affected users deserved accurate information from the outset, and we let them down. We apologize for this error.

Following a comprehensive review, we can now provide an accurate account of the situation.

The Ribbon vaults operated with three distinct pools of funds:
- active funds, deployed weekly to execute the vault strategy;
- queued withdrawals, which consisted of funds that users had already requested to withdraw and were held separately, pending finalization;
- paused funds, not actively allocated nor queued.
Crucially, queued and paused funds remained untouched by the exploit.

The exploit affected only the active funds, which totaled approximately $2.7M across all vaults (including approximately $400K held by the DAO). This active portion has been entirely drained, while the queued and paused funds remain intact.

Approximately $350K in funds are held in the vault pauser contract (paused funds). Users with funds in the pauser contract will be able to recover them in full, however this will require a contract upgrade. We will announce once the upgrade is deployed; in the meantime, please wait.

We understand the implications of what we are about to say, and we do not say it lightly:
- If you had queued a withdrawal prior to the exploit, you may finalize it and recover 100% of your funds. The queue currently holds approximately $4.3M in various assets;
- If you had paused your funds, you'll be able to withdraw them in full, pending a contract update (please wait for our announcement);
- If you had not queued a withdrawal or paused prior to the exploit, your active funds have been entirely lost.

We recognize how devastating this is for those affected. There is no framing that softens a total loss, and we will not pretend otherwise.

Following the exploit, DAO representatives have lodged complaints with the relevant authorities and notified all centralized exchanges that the exploiter has interacted with.
The DAO also remains committed to engaging with its members on potential paths forward for vault depositors. Should you wish to propose a remediation initiative, we encourage you to submit a governance proposal through the established process.

Again, we apologize for the earlier misinformation.

We regret to confirm that the legacy Ribbon DOV vaults were exploited yesterday following a vulnerability in a smart contract update, resulting in a loss of approximately $2.7M USD.

We have immediately taken action to identify the root cause and are coordinating with CEXs and security partners to ensure the stolen funds are tracked and marked. Although the perpetrator bypassed our existing Immunefi bounty, the offer remains open for a potential whitehat resolution.

To Aevo users and stakers: the exchange is not impacted in any way and remains fully secure and operational.

For Ribbon Legacy depositors, we are currently defining the best course of action; please expect an update within the next 24 hours. If you have questions, support is available via DMs or our ticketing system on the exchange.

A full post-mortem will follow shortly. Thank you for your patience as we resolve this.

Rolling daily $SPX GEX snapshots have been somewhat irrelevant since spring 2022.

That's when Tue/Thu SPX expiries were added and 0DTE became an everyday phenomenon. 

A single daily reading aggregates over three properties of today's market that the headline number can't capture:

—————
1) It's intraday-dynamic.

- Three key variables move at once through the session: 
Spot crosses strikes, 
- 0DTE positions are opened, closed and rolled (so dealer inventory itself shifts, not just where spot sits within it), 
- Time decays toward the cash close.

The gamma profile at 10:00 isn't the one at 14:30.

—————
2) It's extremely localized at the strike, and grows quasi-exponentially as expiration approaches.

Same ATM strike, 1h vs 3d to expiry: peak gamma multiple folds higher and the profile far narrower (chart below).

Stack that across every active 0DTE strike near spot and you get the spiky, migratory surface dealers actually hedge.

—————
3) It's not comparable to pre-2022.

Position distribution, the share of risk sitting in 0DTEs, and the speed at which positioning rotates intraday are all structurally different from the weekly/monthly regime that came before.

A 2024 print and a 2019 print aren't measuring the same object.

—————
PS:

What's actually shown is more a proxy for net OI in proximity to spot — naive GEX, with calls assumed bought by MMs and puts sold by them. 

That sign convention was always a shortcut, and in a regime where positioning flips intraday, anchoring to a daily snapshot of it is shakier still.

Friday was OpEx, which gave me a good reason for a defined-risk structure like a put credit spread.

OpEx tends to produce outsized pin-risk, which is favorable for theta. But pins can also break sharply late in the day. The credit spread captures the theta while capping the risk if things turn.

Case study: Friday's $SPY put credit spread for +71%.

Ours doesn’t.

What we built is closer to a coordinated AI system than a bot — a stack of models that actually interpret the market in real time and make decisions together.

A separate model analyzes funding rates, volatility expansion, and cross-venue signals to understand the broader context. And then there’s the execution layer — a model dedicated entirely to timing, entries, and minimizing slippage.

Before any trade is placed on Hyperliquid, the system runs a multi-model consensus. Signals are compared, weighted, and stress-tested internally. If alignment isn’t strong enough, the system simply does nothing.

No forced trades. No overtrading.

Another key part of the system is regime detection.

The AI constantly evaluates what kind of market it’s operating in — whether it’s trending, ranging, volatile, or being manipulated. And based on that, it completely shifts behavior. In strong trends, it leans into momentum. In choppy conditions, it reduces exposure or stays out entirely. In high-risk environments, it prioritizes capital preservation over profit.

This is where most systems fail — they trade the same way in every condition. Ours doesn’t.

It dynamically adjusts position sizing, leverage, entry timing, and scaling strategies in real time. Not based on fixed rules, but based on continuously recalculated risk. Execution itself is another layer most people underestimate.

We built latency-aware routing specifically for Hyperliquid. The system understands when to execute instantly, when to sit passively in the order book, and when to split orders to reduce slippage and improve fills. This isn’t just signal-based trading — it’s execution-aware trading.

And then there’s the feedback loop.

Every trade feeds back into the system. Wins and losses are both used to refine how models interpret order flow, volatility, and liquidity behavior. Over time, the system doesn’t just repeat strategies — it adapts and evolves.

That’s the real difference.

This isn’t a static bot running predefined logic. It’s a live system of interacting AI agents operating inside one of the most liquid perp environments in crypto.

How to stop losing money trading options:

1. Most options expire worthless. If you're only buying options, the math is working against you. Start selling options instead of buying them. Let theta work in your favor, not against you.

2. Stop buying short-dated options. Every single day that passes, your contract loses value. The closer to expiration, the faster it decays. If you're going to buy, buy LEAPs - one year or more until expiration. Time becomes your ally instead of your enemy.

3. Sell options on stocks you actually want to own. Get paid premium while you wait for your price. If the stock drops to your strike, you get assigned at a discount. If it doesn't, you keep the cash and do it again next month.

4. Use charts before every trade. RSI, support levels, moving averages. Whether you're buying or selling, the entry matters. A good strategy with a bad entry is still a losing trade.

5. Stop treating options like lottery tickets. The traders who survive long term aren't hitting home runs. They're collecting singles, managing risk, and letting the framework do the work.

Most people lose money on options because they buy the wrong contracts at the wrong time with no plan. Fix those three things and you fix most of the problem.

Here is my 10-step framework you need to be aware of when buying LEAPS options:

9. Delta matters. A 0.80 delta LEAP moves like 80 shares, not 100. Know what you're actually controlling.

The Daily Fix: Managing risk into mega-cap earnings and a symbolic FOMC meeting

Overnight price action and AI-driven moves

We've seen some pockets of movement overnight in markets, and the technicals and price action evolve in line with the hedging and repositioning ahead of the upcoming key event risk. In US equity, we saw some ripples from the leaked memo about OpenAI failing to meet its revenue projections, and that it may not honour certain contracts if revenue doesn't grow at a faster clip. This caused some outsized moves in names like Oracle, and those companies highly leveraged to OpenAI's ability to generate sufficient cashflow. OpenAI did come back and suggest those fears were overdone, and to be fair, most close to OpenAI's developments would not be overly surprised by what they've heard, given Sam Altman's 'code red' last year. Perhaps, given the run in a number of these AI-related stocks, taking some off the table was possible regardless of any leaked memo - buying weakness in the 2026 winners remains the clear tactical play.

In the art of risk management and achieving optimal position sizing relative to the impactful event risk from earnings in the session ahead, traders and investors are always going to look at positions and exposures, and the possible P&L impact should the company not meet a very high bar.

Implied moves highlight the potential for volatility

The implied volatility and the options implied move on earnings day for the four mega-cap companies speak volumes, with the implied earnings day move for Amazon priced at -/+6.7%, Meta and Microsoft -/+6.6%, and Alphabet -/+5.1%. Given the combined index weighting for these four companies equates to around 20% of the S&P500 weight and over 30% for NAS100, things could get a little funky in the after-hours. The most important factor for these stocks is positioning and crowding, and where the buy side funds, the entities with size holdings and exposures in these stocks, sets their expectations for earnings and guidance, and how they may respond to the guidance.

High expectations leave little room for disappointment

Certainly, in the case of Alphabet and Amazon, the investment community has an outright love affair with these stocks and has piled in, and as such the bar to please is sky high. They will need to blow the lights out in spades, or we could see a real risk of disappointment and an initial downside move on the day. Whether Amazon indeed was to fall 6.7% is debatable, and certainly, if the numbers met sell-side expectations, a 6.7% sell-off would likely entice people to support into weakness.

What matters most in the earnings detail

But the market also needs to understand exactly what parts of the earnings metrics and guidance are specifically targeted in terms of market sensitivity. That can often come down to divisional breakdown, such as AWS growth for Amazon or Azure for Microsoft. Earnings from Microsoft will be of high interest because they will be the only hyperscaler business expected to give FY capex guidance for 2027, with the other three hyperscalers expected to maintain their capex guidance for 2026 at current rates. A big boost to capex for 2027 for Microsoft could set the standard and expectations for the other hyperscalers.

Capex concerns ease as monetisation improves

But what's important is that the market has recently repriced and removed much of the overhang and concerns around the return on investment from the massive capex intentions, even for Meta, which caused angst in their prior quarter report. And people are seeing clearer signs of monetisation of their AI capex spend. A factor that was certainly helped by Amazon CEO Andy Jassy with his recent note to investors talking about AI monetisation, cost discipline, and the margin trajectory.

Oil shrugs off UAE and OPEC developments

The other factor on the day has been the key removal, or the divorce, of the UAE from OPEC and OPEC+. Are we necessarily surprised by this? Perhaps not, and on any other given day, this news may have seen the Brent price move down $5 to $6 off the bat, given the UAE accounts for around 10% of OPEC output. However, with the UAE's production facilities currently close to capacity, it is perhaps no surprise that Brent front-month futures quickly erased the initial drop of $2.12 and settled up over 2% on the day, with oil traders expressing a view of future higher UAE production in the 2027 futures contracts.

A symbolic FOMC meeting ahead

The Federal Reserve meets tonight and lays down its statement. Given the dynamics unfolding in energy markets, a patient stance is warranted and likely what we will get. The meeting will be symbolic in the sense that it will likely be Jerome Powell's last press conference as Chair of the Federal Reserve. The interest rate swaps market sees the Fed's next move not materialising any time soon, and as such, all signs point to this being a low volatility event, with limited event risk for traders to be concerned about.

Focus shifts to Australian inflation data

Focus in Asia today will fall on Australian inflation for March and the updated number for Q1 inflation, as well as pre-positioning in tech and AI names given the flow-on effects from the US earnings reports. For Aussie CPI, we will likely see the full impact of the rise in retail fuel costs in the March inflation data, with headline CPI expected at 4.8% year-on-year, a sharp rise from the February number of 3.7%.

Divergence between headline and trimmed mean
Contrast that with the trimmed mean CPI for March, which is expected at 3.3%. That is quite some divergence, but the RBA will likely look through the headline impact and focus more closely on the Q1 trimmed mean inflation report. The consensus is that the rise is 0.9% quarter-on-quarter, broadly in line with the RBA's forecast, taking it to an annualised rate of 3.5%.

RBA Rate hike expectations 

That in itself does warrant some tightening of policy, and the interest rate swaps market already implies a hike on 5 May at 79%. The risks, I feel, are still skewed to the upside. So, a trimmed mean number at 1% or above on a quarter-on-quarter basis will only solidify those expectations for a hike on 5 May.

Terminal rate still a moving target

What's also important is not just whether we get a hike in May, but the pace of hikes through 2026 and where the cash rate could potentially be taken at a terminal level. The current view is that we could see the cash rate at 4.8% to 5% by the end of the year. That remains a moving target.

AUD supported, euro remains under pressure

While there are some stagflationary forces at work in the Australian economy, they appear manageable and not a genuine market concern at this stage. This does support the Australian dollar to a small extent. Against the euro, outperformance continues, with EUR/AUD looking set to test the recent lows of 1.6150.

Europe growth risks skewed to the downside

Europe may be looking at interest rate hikes, but the high Brent price will have a greater impact. With the ECB's bank lending data showing tighter standards for both households and businesses, and Jamie Dimon warning of credit issues in Europe, the broader Eurozone outlook appears skewed to the downside, and selling rallies seems appropriate.

The Daily Fix: The Message Portrayed in the Crude Futures Curve

The market has been treated to a further barrage of geopolitical headline risk, and this will only remain the case for the days and possibly weeks ahead. But are we becoming somewhat desensitised to the headline risk? I don’t think so. We’re simply becoming more selective in what we react to, focusing on what is tangible in terms of de-escalation or a credible and lasting off-ramp.

There remains increased scepticism around a near-term ceasefire, with the prediction markets now pricing the probability of a ceasefire by the end of April at 31% and by end-May at 47%. These markets also assign just a 25% probability to a normalisation of the Strait of Hormuz by April 30. This is being reflected in today’s price action in the energy markets, with WTI front-month crude futures settling above $100 for the first time in this run, and traders building demand for WTI crude one-month ATM implied volatility, now settling at an impressive 86%.

The introduction of the Houthis into the equation, with Iran seemingly dictating their strategic directive, has put attention on the probability that the Houthis directly attempt to impact Saudi flows into the Red Sea. This development would add further upside risks to front-month crude futures, but importantly across the future-dated crude futures curve. It is the pricing further out the futures curve that makes for an important observation, and what pricing in the further-dated contracts is reflecting.

Attention also builds on the Brent crude December futures contract, which at $84.08 has been far more anchored than the shorter-dated futures contracts, and presents a portrayal of where crude could trade, a possibly loose theoretical fair value, should we see Hormuz functioning to pre-conflict flow. We can also look to the July and August futures contracts, as this part of the curve may offer a more fitting implied probability on how energy traders view ceasefire probabilities, and the functioning of Hormuz. Should Brent crude August futures break above $100, now $94.77, one suspects it would not do any favours for equities, credit, and a broader suite of risk assets.

Taking the timeframe in and reviewing the intraday price action, what stands out is the buy-weakness mindset among energy traders, while equity traders were skewed towards selling rallies in single stocks and index futures. Front-month Brent dipped below $112 going into settlement, before buyers stepped back in post-settlement to push both Brent and WTI higher into the close.

This, in turn, saw the S&P500 futures roll over into US trade. After staging a decent recovery from the lows printed in early Asia, trading up towards 6,481, sellers once again took control, pushing both cash and futures markets lower. The real stress was evident in small caps, with the Russell 2000 cash closing down 1.5% and below the 200-day moving average for the first time since January 2025.

If traders are rotating out of the lower-quality end of the equity spectrum, this aligns with developments in fixed income markets, where US Treasury yields fell 8 to 9 basis points across the curve. Part of this move has been driven by a modestly dovish shift at the margin from Fed Chair Powell, but the renewed buying in Treasuries suggests markets are re-embracing their defensive qualities, even as short-term inflation swaps continue to rise.

While Treasury yields have fallen sharply, this has not weighed on the dollar, with the USD well bid across the G10 FX spectrum. The dollar index is now breaking out of the upper end of the range it has held since May 2025, and at 100.57, the question is whether this move can build into a continuation of the bull trend that began in February.

Looking at the dollar index requires a view on EUR/USD, currently trading at 1.1456. For the dollar to truly extend higher, we would likely need to see a break below 1.14. Given the weighting of the yen in the DXY basket, a move higher in USDJPY, ideally back above 160, would also help, although that remains challenging given perceived intervention risks from the MOF, and the lower possibility that Scott Bessent is again checking rates...

Within the FX complex, the heavier moves are coming through in sterling. GBP/USD is now trading below 1.32, having firmly broken the March 12 low of 1.3218. The dollar, more broadly, continues to look well supported, with notable strength also seen against the Swedish krona, which has broken above recent highs and is now threatening the October to November supply zone around 9.5834.

The rally in the US dollar, despite falling Treasury yields, speaks to its safe-haven appeal within G10, a dynamic that cannot be dismissed, particularly if the S&P continues to trend lower and small caps remain under pressure.

Gold has found some stability, up 0.4% to $2,450, but the more telling move is gold priced in non-USD currencies. When priced in the weaker currencies, taking the USD out of the equation, gold has shown solid upside, particularly against sterling. That gold is rising alongside a firmer dollar is notable, with support coming from falling nominal and real yields.

"External finance premium: market finance versus bank finance," by Livia Chiţu, Sofia Gori, and Refet S. Gürkaynak.

"This paper is the first to simultaneously examine firms’ market-based and bank-based external finance premia and investigate the behavior of corporate bond markets in the United States and the euro area, with a focus on country- and state-level heterogeneity in monetary unions. Using a unique micro-level dataset, we show that market finance premia, measured with corporate bond spreads, are remarkably similar in both the euro area and the US in terms of how little they depend on the issuer’s state or country of origin. In neither monetary union is the transmission of monetary policy to corporate bond rates differentiated as a function of the state or country of issuer. Unconditionally, the state or country of origin of the bond issuers explains very little of the variance among corporate bond spreads, in stark contrast to bank loan spreads that are determined at the country level for the same sample of bond-issuing firms. The euro area corporate bond market is as integrated as the US one, contrary to conventional beliefs. The marked difference between country influences on bank loan and corporate debt spreads is not due to selection effects in bond issuing firms but owes directly to the nature of market finance."

"The Central Bank’s Dilemma: Look Through Supply Shocks or Control Inflation Expectations?" by Paul Beaudry, Thomas J Carter, and Amartya Lahiri.

"When countries are hit by supply shocks, central banks often face the dilemma of either looking through such shocks or reacting to them to ensure that inflation expectations remain anchored. In this paper, we propose a tractable framework to capture this dilemma and explore optimal policy under various assumptions on how agents form their expectations and the sophistication with which those expectations account for the central bank’s announced policies. While our analysis covers a wide range of potential specifications, our baseline results focus on level-k thinking (LKT) – a form of bounded rationality that enjoys significant support in the experimental literature and encompasses both adaptive expectations (AE) and rational expectations (RE) as special cases. Nonetheless, we show that the optimal policy under LKT is qualitatively very different from its analogues under AE and RE, exhibiting abrupt pivots in the policy stance. In particular, it is optimal for the central bank to initially look through supply shocks until a threshold is reached, then pivot discontinuously to a more hawkish anti-inflationary stance. We find that such pivots can, if optimally executed, be compatible with soft landings in the sense that most (or even all) of the reduction in inflation occurs through re-anchoring of expectations rather than economic slack. We also discuss risks and why policy errors in terms of tightening too late or too slowly can be especially costly in such an environment."
